analysis.one_liner: Limits courts' ability to seal evidence of public health and safety dangers in civil case settlements.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Judiciary Committee in 2008 without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When companies settle lawsuits, they often require the other side to keep everything secret — including evidence that a drug, car, or product is dangerous. Those secrecy deals are usually approved by a judge. This bill would tell federal courts to stop approving them when public health or safety is at stake, unless the judge finds a specific, substantial reason for secrecy, and it would guarantee that people can still report hazards in a case to government regulators. It was introduced in the House in April 2008, sent to the Judiciary Committee, and never received a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, patients, and workers benefit if the bill passes: information about dangerous drugs, vehicles, products, and workplaces revealed in court cases could no longer be buried under court-approved secrecy. Regulators, journalists, other plaintiffs, and the public would learn about hazards earlier, because the person who settled the case could talk about the evidence and report it to government agencies.

how_it_helps.text: It bars courts from sealing records or issuing protective orders that hide information about public health or safety risks unless the judge specifically finds secrecy is justified and keeps the order no broader than necessary.
It prevents companies from demanding secrecy as a condition of producing documents in discovery, which is how many broad gag orders currently originate.

It says courts cannot enforce settlement terms that stop a party from reporting safety information to any federal or state regulator, so hazards discovered in a lawsuit could still reach the agencies charged with protecting the public.

It lets parties talk about the fact of a settlement and the evidence in a case, though it allows the dollar amount to stay confidential and protects individuals' personal financial and health information with a presumption of privacy.

analysis.who_pays: Companies facing lawsuits — drug makers, device makers, automakers, and other product manufacturers — would pay. Secret settlements are a standard tool for containing litigation costs and reputational damage; this bill would take that tool away whenever the secret concerns health or safety, exposing them to bad publicity, more lawsuits from similarly injured people, and regulatory action.

drawbacks.text: The bill could expose trade secrets and competitively sensitive business information along with health and safety hazards, since the court must weigh disclosure against only a 'specific and substantial interest' in secrecy.

It creates a presumption that a person's financial, health, or similar personal information stays confidential, but courts would still have to litigate these questions case by case, adding cost and delay to settlements.

Critics of such measures have long argued that private parties should be free to settle on confidential terms, and that federalizing settlement terms intrudes on the courts' traditional control of their own dockets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large: fewer court-sanctioned gag orders means regulators, journalists, and future plaintiffs can learn about dangerous products from people who were harmed by them. The cost is privacy: without the carve-out, trade secrets, personal financial details, and medical information revealed in litigation could be exposed more broadly, which could make companies less willing to hand over sensitive records during discovery. The bill also does nothing to private settlements reached without a court order, so its reach depends on parties actually going to court. On balance, the public-health benefit outweighs the privacy cost, and the bill's own presumption tries to contain the privacy problem.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee and then to two of its subcommittees, where no hearing or vote ever happened, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 23, 2008 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day.
On June 3, 2008 it was referred to two Judiciary subcommittees, and no further action of any kind was taken for the rest of the two-year Congress.
The bill never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or a companion Senate push, and expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies facing lawsuits over dangerous products, and their insurers, are better off: they kept their ability to settle cases under court-approved secrecy, so evidence of health and safety hazards stays buried. The public continues to bear the cost in hazards it cannot learn about.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies hiding hazards; the public stayed uninformed

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (Chair John Conyers, D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, no vote, no report — and later sent it to two subcommittees, where it also sat without action.

against.name: Corporate defendants and liability insurers
against.role: Industries that rely on confidential settlements
against.what_they_did: Have long opposed Sunshine in Litigation-type measures through industry lobbying, arguing confidential settlements protect trade secrets and privacy.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; all four sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, and the Democratic-run Judiciary Committee declined to move the bill, so the record shows no partisan contest, only inaction.

industries.industry: Litigation-prone manufacturers (drug, medical device, auto, consumer products)
industries.note: Defendants in product-liability and malpractice cases currently use protective orders and confidential settlements to keep evidence of injuries and hazards out of public view. The bill would strip that tool, exposing them to bad publicity, copycat lawsuits, and regulator follow-up when a settlement reveals a genuine safety problem.

Liability insurers rely on confidential settlements to cap and contain claims. Some information they currently keep sealed — details of repeated safety failures — could become disclosable, weakening their leverage in negotiations.

Plaintiffs' lawyers and injured parties would gain leverage: defendants could no longer demand broad secrecy as the price of a settlement, and hazards unearthed in litigation could be shared with regulators and the public.
